Independent finite replay: group j³+k³ by exact integer sum for all 1≤j≤k≤24, retaining only groups with at least two pairs; for a prefix N retain only pairs with k≤N and regroup. The fibers are 1729: (1,12),(9,10); 4104: (2,16),(9,15); 13832: (2,24),(18,20).
correctness.rationale: Haar orthogonality applied to F² gives 2S²−Σ|a|⁴ plus 8 times the real part of the coefficient-product pairing for each of the two exceptional fibers; the off-diagonal multiplicity is two. Normalize S=1. For fixed mass on the shared vertex and each three-vertex arm, equal weights within each arm simultaneously optimize the positive product and negative square sum. At a fixed shared mass with 0<x<1, the derivative for the split between arms factors as √z−√(1−z) times a strictly increasing bracket on (1/2,1), so no unbalanced interior split can maximize. At the balanced split, multiplying the gap from 9/4 by 12(1+y²)² gives the strictly positive quartic in (4); expanding its two squares leaves the stated positive constant 1169/1296. At a one-arm endpoint, the square sum and AM–GM give 9/4 with exactly four equal weights; the phase correction must attain its modulus. Shared mass 0 or 1 cannot give equality. Scaling the seven-vertex bound by the square of the mass on the union forces zero mass outside the union in equality. Independent exact pair grouping found only 1729 and 4104 through index 23, with first indices 12 and 16 and shared mode 9, and the additional 13832 at 24. The zero-collision case gives 2−1/N by the square-sum inequality, and the one-collision range uses the four-weight bound. This checks the fourth power of the norm constant, not the constant before taking the fourth power.

value.rationale: The first pair of interacting resonances sharing a character is a natural test of whether coexistence improves the sharp norm. The result answers no and proves that optimizing coefficients suppress an entire arm; it is not merely a recomputation of known cubic identities. Positive cubes exhibit precisely this configuration and give the sharp finite plateau.
